attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the correct coordinates into the [place sprite on top of] block so that the Player sprite starts on the green tile on the top left?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the tilemap design? 

❓ How is using a tilemap different from setting a background color or image?

❓ What happens when you try to move the Player sprite through a wall?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to notice the components of the tilemap. Similar to creating a background image, the editor allows the ninja to use pixel squares to create a design. In a tilemap, the ninja is able to place sprites directly in the tilemap design and establish walls that serve as an additional barrier for the sprites to move around.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by setting the Player sprite’s position on the tilemap! 


Open Scene and drag a [place sprite on top of] block into the [on start] container underneath the Player sprite’s [set sprite to] block and above its [move sprite with buttons] block.


Set the Player sprite’s starting position coordinates by typing “1” in the column parameter and “1” in the row parameter.


Click ▶ to explore the tilemap by moving the Player sprite around the screen. What do you notice happens when the Player sprite interacts with the different tiles?

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click “My Tiles”, then replace the green tiles on the tilemap with the blue path tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the different colored tiles? 

❓ What do you think the red-tinted tiles represent?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to observe the different parts of the tilemap editor. Many of the icons are similar to ones they’ve already seen when creating sprites or background images. Point the ninja towards the lower left corner to identify the size of the tilemap, denoted by the number of columns and rows there are.

💡Help the ninja identify the different tilemap tiles in the menu on the left side of the screen. Point out that the ninja eventually be able to create their own tilemap using pre-created tiles from the “Gallery” or by creating their own, using the “My Tiles” section.
steps.instructions:
Take a peek inside the tilemap!


Click the square in the [set tilemap to] block to see how different tiles make up the floor and walls of this project.


Close the instructions panel, then look in the lower left corner of the editor to see the size of the tilemap, shown by the number of columns and the number of rows of tiles there are. These values can be adjusted to change the size of the tilemap. 


Notice that the tile used as the Player sprite’s starting position is green instead of blue. Make the green tile match the blue path tiles by clicking “My Tiles'' in the menu on the left side. Select the matching blue tile. Then, click on the green tile square on the tilemap and replace it with the blue one. 


Click “done” to see the new tilemap design on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you type the column and row coordinates you found in the tilemap editor into the Goal sprite’s [place sprite on top of] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you select a blue tile in the bottom right corner of the tilemap to be the Goal sprite’s starting position?

❓ How is setting a sprite’s position on a tilemap similar and different to how you’ve previously set its position on a regular background? How is it different?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to notice how a sprite’s position on a tilemap is designated by the column and row in which a tile is placed on the map, whereas previously, the ninja has used a sprite’s x and y values to set its position on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Set the Goal sprite’s position by adding a [place sprite on top of] block underneath its [set sprite to] block. 


Then, click the square in the [set tilemap to] block. Close the instructions panel, then move your mouse over different squares to see their coordinates (column, row) in the lower left corner.


Hover the cursor over a blue tile in the bottom right corner of the tilemap that will be the Goal sprite’s starting position. Find the square’s coordinates, click “done”, and add the values into the column and row bubbles in the [place sprite on top of] block.


Click ▶ to see the Goal sprite’s starting position on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a row value that places both Enemy sprites’ starting positions on a blue tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What row should the Enemy sprites start at? Do you want them to start on the same or different rows?

❓ Did you click on the square in the [set tilemap to] block to identify the row where each Enemy sprite should be placed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to think about where the Enemy sprites should be placed to create a barrier for the Player sprite to pass through. Encourage the ninja to use the tilemap editor to hover their mouse over a specific tile and identify its row using the coordinates in the lower left corner.
steps.instructions:
Set the Enemy sprites’ starting positions!


Drag out two [place sprite on top of] blocks and add one block under each of the Enemy [set sprite to] blocks. Type “3” into the column parameter of the first Enemy sprite, and “6” into the column parameter of the second Enemy sprite. 


Then, select a row for the Enemy sprites to start at and type a value into the row parameter of each block. Remember, you can click the square in the [set tilemap to] block and move your mouse over different tiles to find their coordinates.


Click ▶ to see Enemy sprites start in different positions on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place the [set sprite velocity] and [set sprite bounce on wall] blocks in the correct sequence with the correct sprite names?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What would you do if you wanted the Enemy sprites to move faster? What if you wanted them to move slower?

❓ How does the [set sprite bounce on wall] block work differently in a tilemap? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to think about the correct sequence of the blocks, ensuring that the [set sprite velocity to] and [set sprite bounce on wall] come after the Enemy sprites and positions have been set.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprites to be moving targets!


Drag out two [set sprite velocity to] blocks. Allow the Enemy sprites to only move up and down by changing the vx value to 0. Place each [set sprite velocity to] block underneath the Enemy sprites’ [place sprite on top of] blocks.


Then, make the Enemy sprites move continuously by bouncing on the tilemap’s walls. Drag out two [set sprite bounce on wall] blocks and set the toggle to <ON>. Place each [set sprite bounce on wall] block underneath the Enemy sprites’ [set sprite velocity to] blocks.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites move up and down on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you select the draw walls   tool in the tilemap editor and click each of the four purple tiles to make them walls?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How is setting walls similar and different to changing the color of a tile?

❓ Why might adding walls be helpful to your project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide the ninja through the different icons in the tilemap editor. The rectangle on the left allows the ninja to create or edit tiles in the tilemap, whereas the 3D draw walls tool on the right allows the ninja to select existing tiles to act as walls.
steps.instructions:
Notice where the Enemy sprites bounced off the walls and changed directions; the purple tiles at the top and bottom of the Enemy sprites’ paths aren’t acting as walls! Change that using the tilemap editor. 


Click the square in the [set tilemap to] block. Then, on the left side menu, click the draw walls icon . After, click on each of the four purple tiles to convert them into walls.


Click “done” and then ▶ to see the Enemy sprites bounce off the walls in the correct location!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a [set life to] block in the [on start] container and a [change life by] block in the correct [on sprite overlaps sprite] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What else could happen when the Player sprite overlaps with an Enemy sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to make sure they’ve selected the correct sprite kind in the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container and set and changed variables in the correct containers.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite!


Add code to make the Player sprite lose a life when it overlaps with an Enemy by adding [set life to] and [change life by] blocks into the correct containers.


Click ▶ to see if the Player can reach the Goal sprite before it overlaps with an Enemy sprite!

steps.hints: 💡 Look back at the Player sprite’s [place sprite on top of] block in the [on start] container to find the Player sprite’s starting column and row values.
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the Player sprite lose all of their lives on overlap with an Enemy sprite?

❓ Why does resetting the Player sprite’s position resolve this bug?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja understand that unless the Player is moved, it will continue to lose lives while overlapped with an Enemy sprite. Therefore, they need to be separated immediately to make the Player lose only one life.

💡 The ninja can also duplicate the Player sprite’s [place sprite on top of] starting position block by right clicking and selecting “duplicate” from the menu.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite immediately loses all of their lives when they overlap with an Enemy sprite! 


Separate the Player and Enemy sprites right away by resetting the Player sprite’s position. Drag a [place sprite on top of] block into the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container. Use a (sprite) bubble from the container as the sprite’s name, then set the coordinates to the Player sprite’s starting position (using the columns and rows). 


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite return to start when it overlaps with an Enemy sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add fun customizations such as dialog text, animations, sounds, etc?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this game by adding directions at the beginning, animating sprites, and experimenting with animating sprites and/or adding music or screen effects.


Click ▶ to see the completed game project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses a tilemap and sets the sprite’s locations using tilemap coordinates!

validationItems.text: Set the Player, Goal, and Enemy sprites’ starting positions using coordinates on the tilemap
Edit a tile on the tilemap
Change the Player sprite’s position and decrease the life variable when the Player and Enemy sprites overlap.
Code the Enemy sprites to move on their own and bounce on tilemap walls.
Edit the walls on the tilemap.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about using tilemaps in your projects. You’ll also review sequence, which is the specific order of steps in code.
